as we all know, very low, something like 10 or 12-1- per cent, probably the lowest that is placed upon any commodity. That there is a monopoly cannot be maintained, because last year some twelve or thirteen million dollars' worth was imported into Canada.
I know the argument is brought that we ought to reduce the tariff on the implements of production. I have thought that over. I have not just been able to grasp the point as well as I might. Perhaps I am dull of comprehension, but I do say this, that the man who operates the plough or a binder, or who is engaged in the industry of fishing in the Maritime provinces, or who is in any way engaged in any of these primary industries, cannot follow his occupation without wearing warm clothing, boots and shoes, eat good food and have many of the other things that enter into our civilized life. For that reason, as I say, I cannot understand why there should be any discrimination as between agricultural implements and any other commodity that is manufactured in Canada. For that reason I should just like-it may not be necessary-to caution the government to go slowly in the matter. If, as I believe, no great good can come from the possible annihilation of an industry now in this country without benefiting anyone. I should say they would do well to go slowly in the matter. In a general way I should like to advocate a policy of considerable caution in a time of uncertainty and depression, lest it might easily be worse. The tariff is not perfect. I believe that the whole tariff structure ought to be overhauled. Three years ago we were supposed to have that brought about. We had a tariff commission, or a tariff committee of the government, go out through the country gathering information but nothing further was ever done. We should have a tariff commission, which might become permanent that would go out and come in with a report, and with information that would enable us to frame a proper tariff. That, if it could not be called a national policy, I might perhaps call a rational policy.
I should like, just in conclusion, to bring one other phase of the matter before the members of this House. I have thought of it a great deal and I see no solution except possibly^ a tariff solution of the question. I have said that I cannot argue with the man who says that the consumer in Canada is entitled absolutely to buy his commodities at the lowest possible price no matter where they may be produced. But I should like to put this situation before the members of the House, and it is not an imaginary one. It exists in

fact to-day, and is being aggravated from day to day. In the countries of Europe and Asia-to-day commodities can be manufactured a great deal more cheaply than they can be made in Canada.

We are shipping immense
quantites of wheat to Europe, and we must be paid for that. What return are we going to get for the commodities we send to Europe? How are be going to get paid for them?

I am not now arguing for a prohibitory tariff. I have never done so, I am not proposing to do so now. I am placing before you a condition that confronts us, a condition with which we will have to deal in some way or other. There can be manufactured in England, in Germany, perhaps in France, I know in Italy, and in Japan, articles for from one-quarter to one-half and two-thirds of the price for which they can be made in this country. And they can be so manufactured and sold in Canada because of currency depreciation for one thing and the other-and I want to deal more particularly with it-the fact that wages are much lower in those countries. Now, I want to say here that I am not in favour of reducing the wage of the Canadian worker, and I do not say that with any ulterior motive at all. I have been a worker myself and I know that the Canadian worker is not paid too much for his toil. He is entitled to receive a wage that will enable him and his family to live in comfort, to have a few pleasures, and to lay by a bit for his old age and for a rainy day. That principle, I think, ought to receive the support of every member of the House. Now if I am right that these goods can be manufactured at an infinitely cheaper price or cost than they can be in this country, if they are admitted to Canada on an equality or without any restrictions-I will put it that way, if they can be admitted to this country without any restrictions whatever-this result will follow; that Canadian made goods cannot be sold; that Canadian factories will become idle; and that Canadian workmen will be out of a job. I am just stating the fact,

and I would like to ask what is the solution of that condition?

My answer to that would
be that at the present moment the Canadian manufacturer is not making any particular complaint with regard to competition from the United States-I do not think so, and I have some one hundred and fifty or od1'-hundred and seventy-five manufacturing establishments in the riding from which I come-but he does say that the competition from the sweat shops, if you like, of Europe is more than he can compete with. We have in the province of Ontario-and this may be news possibly to some of my hon. friends-we have in the province of Ontario what is known as the minimum wage law. countries. I believe such a law is good in principle. There is a condition I am pointing out. But for myself I must say that I am not in favour of anything that will pit the workingman of my constituency against the cheap sweat shop labour of a foreign country, where people are living under conditions under which they should not live.
I may just for a few moments, Mr. Speaker, refer to a specific commodity,-and we are always more or less interested if concrete examples are given,-and that is the commodity of boots and shoes. There are some ten or twelve boot and shoe factories in the riding I represent. To-day, because of the rate of exchange, because of difference in wages, large quantities of boots and shoes are being imported from Great Britain. The ordinary duty on boots and shoes, is I think, 30 per cent. On account of the preferential tariff, that duty is reduced to something like 17J per cent. I do not think the boot and shoe worker is over-paid, and I believe our boot and shoe manufacturing establishments are operated efficiently. The average wage of the shoe worker in my city, and I think throughout Ontario, is something like $23 a week. In Britain the wage is in the neighbourhood of $12 or $13. Then there is a difficulty with which our manufacturers are confronted. The depreciated currency of the European countries operates against them. A suggestion has been made-and it appeals to me-that in connection with importations it would be fair, that on those goods, when they enter a Canadian port, instead of the duty being based on the depreciated currency, it should be based on a fair valuation of the commodity in Canadian territory.
I wish to say a word or two upon what is perhaps a delicate subject, the preferential tariff. It has not been mentioned to any extent. When that tariff was introduced 1 suppose it was for reasons which seemed quite sufficient at that time. I suppose my friends opposite are in favour of a preferential tariff on the score of sentiment. Perhaps they are.
Yes.
Very good. I thought possibly they were in favour of it because it led in the direction of free trade.
Both.

The point I am trying to
make is that there is no sentiment or very little sentiment in business. Trade and commerce are carried on between individuals on a basis of value for value.

The Address-Mr. Euler

That is the principle we
believe in.

And to get something for
something. I say that is the principle upon which individuals trade, and I do not see any reason why nations should depart from that principle. These questions ought to be settled on their merits. I do not think there is any doubt that Britain herself deals with these questions on their merits. As my hon. friend suggested a moment ago, Britain placed an embargo on Canadian cattle, and they had a perfect right to do so, and we had no right to take offence, except for the fact that the reason that was given by them for that embargo was not the real reason. The embargo was placed on Canadian cattle ostensibly to protect British cattle from disease, but the real reason was to protect the breeder of British cattle. Last summer the Prime Minister attended the Imperial Conference at London. At that conference, as hon. members know, the former British Prime Minister, Mr. Baldwin, made a suggestion of a preference within the Empire. Hon. members all know what happened. At the elections Mr. Baldwin and all his policies were rejected by the British people. I say that only to emphasize the fact that the people of the Mother Country are legislating entirely in their own interests, and I am sure that, with the spirit of British fair play that exists there, they can have no possible objections if we legislate in exactly the same way. When 1 entered upon this subject, I said it was perhaps a delicate subject, and I am going to leave it with these words-that it matters little to the Canadian manufacturer, if his British brother puts him out of business rather than his American cousin, or anyone else on the face of the earth; the result is exactly the same.
I have spoken longer than I intended, and perhaps some of what I have said is entirely premature. My position finally is this, that I favour a tariff such as will assist us in the raising of our revenue, and a tariff that will enable us to maintain industries that are legitimate in every way. I hope the government will bear that in mind when framing any tariff policies they may have in contemplation.
I represent a constituency with an industrial population of thousands of people. Towards these workmen as well as the farmers in my constituency I feel a very keen sense of responsibility. My pledge to them at the elections of 1921 was to guard their interests to the best of my ability. That pledge I mean to keep according to my best judg-
ment, and that pledge is not inconsistent with the declarations made by the leaders of the present government in the elections of 1921, that if they were returned to power no legitimate industry would be injured. I received, Sir, last year in good faith, and with approval the declaration of the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) who I wish were here, that henceforth there should be reasonable stability of tariff. I would still commend that to the government as a good policy to follow.
